utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is there any follow-up on what we discussed yesterday, witness scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There is. Firstly in relation to DST-060, we would like to make an application, an oral application for a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And may I take it that it is based on the same grounds as the application -- the earlier application as a matter of fact which ended up in a summons? Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I did foreshadow this earlier but didn't make an application. This was probably three weeks ago. I did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, yes, yes. I might mix up at this moment. We'll have -- yes, the -- we heard yesterday that the Prosecution would not oppose the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The basis seems to that the witness seems to be reluctant or, at least, refuses to come and testify, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not object either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything you would like to add to this, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think with the threshold criteria, I think Your Honours, unless Your Honours need to hear further in relation to the attempts we've made, the second threshold material is that the witness's information may materially assist the case and our submissions have been laid out when we made the application for a videolink, so they are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we rely on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter. We'll do it with priority. If we would need any further information, then we'll first seek that information through informal means to be put on the record at a later stage. I repeat, if.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is there anything else? If not, could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Whilst the witness is being brought into court, perhaps we could just deal with one other matter which needs to be dealt with at some point. In relation to the witnesses that Your Honours issued the decision on yesterday, the 92 bis now no longer 92 bis, having considered the matter overnight and consulted with our client, we have decided not to proceed with those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Neither of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither of them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We apologise for what might seem like a waste of judicial resources considering the issue, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have considered it. The decision is there and the Chamber decided for both the same and gave some suggestions for one of them, but you have now decided not to call either of them. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I just inquire as to the third who was part of that application who was a 92 quater, whether this only applies to the 92 bis witnesses or also to the 92 quater witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, for 92 bis and 92 ter, of course it's relevant whether you call the witnesses or not. Of course for a 92 quater witness, that is not an issue, at least not for this 92 quater witness, I wouldn't say never for any of them. But I think Mr. Jordash clearly referred to the two witnesses on which the Chamber had decided yesterday and I think I announced yesterday that we would postpone, or at least we would give our decision for the third one, at a later stage. So I understood it not to be covered by your observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragicevic. First of all, apologies for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, apologies for being so impolite as to continue our conversation when you are entering the courtroom. Mr. Dragicevic, I would like to remind you again that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, the solemn declaration you gave --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on Tuesday. Mr. Farr will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Farr, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: To start with I want to clarify one thing I think may have been incorrectly recorded in the transcript yesterday. Can you just confirm that the uniforms you saw Rajo Bozovic, Zika Ivanovic and the other special unit veterans wearing in the video of the Kula ceremony that we watched yesterday are the same uniforms as the uniform that you saw Franko Simatovic wearing and the other members of the DB escort wearing during the hostage negotiations in 1995? Is it correct that those are the same uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. When we stopped yesterday we were discussing the relationship between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Milosevic. In paragraph 87 of your statement you discuss one aspect of that relationship, specifically the reason for Mr. Stanisic's dismissal. You say: [As read] "There were a lot of talks in public and press about the dismissal of Stanisic in 1998. It was said and written that Stanisic had a clash with the Milosevic family. I think that the direct cause was direct clash regarding the solving problems in Kosovo." In paragraph 88 of your statement you say: [As read] "Stanisic believed that the Kosovo crisis could be resolved by political means through negotiations and agreement and not by war."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can we now please have 65 ter 477 -- sorry, 4777.1 on the screen. This document is a set of meeting minutes from meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in 1998. This is a selection from a larger document of only those minutes that are relevant to DB involvement in Kosovo and this document was received from the Serbian government on the 19th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, it's the Prosecution position that you are incorrect regarding Stanisic's views on Kosovo. I'm going to show you a few excerpts from the minutes of meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and then ask you whether they affect your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have page 5 in English and page 5 in B/C/S around the middle of the page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that we have technical difficulties. When the Registrar says to me that the system is down, it must be serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the problem has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, these are the meetings -- sorry, these are the minutes of a meeting of the Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command from the 2nd of August, 1998, and I'm interested here in the comments of Mr. Gajic. First of all, can you confirm that a man named David Gajic was a senior official of the Serbian DB at this time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic is recorded as saying: [As read] "Legija from the line tt trig point 751 to Istrelov vrh tt-728 and Krstovo Brdo [phoen] and Raponja [phoen] Rakitnica. The aim is to seal off Lausa. They reached the mosque in Lausa." At the continuation of the meeting just below, he seems to say: "The JSO and the 4th Detachment entered Lausa. The 3rd Detachment is at this former lines. Move two companies to the 4th Detachment in order to reach Ovcarevo more quickly. No."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could now have the next page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This page shows the minutes from the meeting the next day, the 3rd of August, 1998. And at the beginning General Pavkovic is recorded as saying: "Frenki and everyone go to Likovac tomorrow." And then on the bottom half of the page Mr. Radovic says "the Franko special unit, it is," and then something was unclear to the translator, "going to between Drenica and /illegible/ Mahala."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could now have page 8 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This page reflects that these are the minutes from the 12 August 1998 meeting and that Jovica Stanisic was also present.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we can have the next page, we'll see what Mr. Stanisic says.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I'll read it just in part. Among other things he says: [As read] "Send the DB units from Lodza to Rausic had the offensive not been" -- then a word that was illegible to the translator, "we would be having big problems and it's part of a resolute stand by JV. We shouldn't fool ourselves, the centres have not been cleaned. We need more successes." Just below that we see Mr. Sainovic say: "The DB should cover and take over this third zone." And "the DB and the army should jointly come up with ideas for what to do next." Finally on the bottom half of the next page in both languages, Mr. Minic is recorded as saying: [As read] "We have crushed their military power part is in the towns, part in Albania and part has been killed." He then lists under important points at number 2: "Find the terrorists, keep flushing them out and liquidating." And then in "(DB)". There are other similar quotes in the other minutes in this document but I think that this is a fair representation of them. Sir, the Prosecution position is that these minutes show that you are wrong when you say that Mr. Stanisic favoured a political solution in Kosovo rather than a war. What is your response to that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I begin, I would like to draw attention to the Prosecution and the Honourable Chamber to the fact that I did not participate in those events and I haven't seen this document before. As for my statement that Mr. Stanisic based his main views on the basis of resolving the crisis through negotiations and agreements rather than through war, when I use the word "war" I did not have in mind global meaning of the words but rather combat against KLA terrorist units with all the means available to our country and our state. What happened here is something to do exclusively with the struggle against Albanian terrorist formations and one should understand it solely in that way. In my view, Mr. Stanisic's position was also to try and find a solution through talks with normal and reasonable people with a view to putting a stop to all the events and chaos that prevailed in Kosovo at the time. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, you've just made a reference to -- well, you said: "When I use the word war I did not have in mind global meaning of the words but rather combat against KLA terrorist units with all the means available to our country and state." The last quote that I read, which is spoken by a Mr. Minic, but at a meeting where Jovica Stanisic is present, he lists under important points at number 2: "Find the terrorists, keep flushing them out and liquidating" then in "(DB)." Sir, doesn't that indicate that Jovica Stanisic supported and, in fact, was involved in the execution of precisely what you are talking about, combat against KLA terrorist units as you describe them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was exactly the purpose for having our anti-terrorist unit, that would be used in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So your evidence is that when you said that Mr. Stanisic was, in your view, opposed to war in Kosovo, that didn't include opposition to combat between the DB special unit and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to understand that we perceived and understood KLA units to be terrorist units. For that reason we used our anti-terrorist units exclusively in fighting with them and not fighting the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, just for my understanding, you say Mr. Stanisic preferred peaceful solutions rather than war. And you said but KLA those were terrorists, that's not war. Who else was there? What military units were there else than the KLA to even consider to go at war with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know they were the only ones. There was our army. As for the view held by Mr. Stanisic that these two -- these means of combatting terrorists should also be used, well, they are the means used world-wide but it does not mean that one needs to resort to them at all costs. One also needed to engage in discussions with those who one could speak to down there, engage terrorist units and that was the way to go about it. But it was not a struggle against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course you -- to conduct war against a civilian population is not exactly what one would expect an army to do, isn't it? You don't go at war with the civilian population, you go at war with the armed forces of the other party and if I understood you well, the only armed forces you could fight against in Kosovo was the KLA, but you have now added to your answer that it was not only the -- targeting the KLA, but also to seek ways of peaceful negotiations, is that how I have to understand your answer, that both tracks were on the mind of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. Of course, an army is not used against the civilian population. It is only used against alien or foreign armed forces. That was where Milosevic made a mistake later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's another matter. Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, just one more question on this matter. You just said: "An army is not used against the civilian population it's only used against alien or foreign armed forces." Isn't that the definition of a war, or have I misunderstood you somehow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, but he also said -- sorry to jump up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, while, Mr. Jordash, you may object against the question, but to add to the question is not what -- if you say could you please add what he said in line so and so, then Mr. Farr can decide what he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not for you to add to his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, you are right. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you would like Mr. Farr to add something to his question or give more context?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Farr missed out the essential sentence which was the sentence immediately after the witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, would you consider to rephrase your question in light of what Mr. Jordash just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fact I think I'm happy to leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And at this point I would tender 65 ter 47771 -- 4777.1 as a Prosecution exhibit. It contains minutes from meetings on six different days. In the interest of time we've only used excerpts from three of those days but the remaining three are relevant to the same point and we offer this only for impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do object insofar as the document that we have before us is not minutes. These are notes made by one of the individuals who took part in the meeting. We feel it is inappropriate to call the document "minutes" and we do feel it is inappropriate to have it admitted in the file in view of the nature of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Farr would say that he seeks admission of the notes taken at these meetings, would that change your position, Mr. Petrovic? And second question would be, does it go to admissibility, and if so, please explain, or does it go to weight?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it goes primarily to the weight that can be attached to the document, but also in terms of how far the answers can be -- given by the witness can be helpful since the questions as termed when put to the witness characterise the document as minutes, and that was how the witness answered these questions. And, of course, it adds to -- terming the document as "minutes" adds to the weight of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the questions that were put to the witness, I think did not focus on whether you would call them minutes or notes. As a matter of fact, he was asked whether what was contained in that document, whether the substance did change his mind and I asked a few questions in relation to the answers he gave to Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, the contents of the document are unreliable, unverified and on the basis of unreliable and unverified notes, the witness was asked to answer a number of questions. That's the basis of my objection in relation to the document itself, the way it was used with the witness and in light of what the witness had to comment on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, you've seen the document which certainly does not appear as a verbatim record of what was said. Would your questions -- would your answers have been any different if Mr. Farr would not have called them minutes but notes where they appear to be notes rather than verbatim minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already said that this is the first time I'm seeing the minutes. However, I cannot give any valuable answers because I didn't attend the meeting, nor was I part of that team. I can only give my opinion on the matter and say what the way was that Mr. Stanisic believed the crisis in Kosovo could really be resolved. So I can comment on the document but I don't know how helpful I can be in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I spoke too soon. Having taken instructions, we also object to the document. Our position is that it is not authentic. It has Mr. Stanisic present in August of 1998 and he was not present in the relevant location at that time. In fact, he was in Greece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that the document will be -- authenticity seems to be a matter which we should look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The authenticity of course, of a document -- first, Mr. Farr, I give you an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Just briefly, in terms of authenticity, this document was received from the government of Serbia and it's our position that that's sufficient authentication for the purposes of admission. Obviously other concerns about authenticity can go to weight. In response to Mr. Petrovic's distinction between minutes and notes, I think he concedes that it's a record of the meeting, whatever it's called. It's offered for purposes of impeachment. It's not offered as the basis for a conviction. And the Chamber will weigh the document against the witness's evidence on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, of course I see the document also for the first time today. Where is the location of the meeting mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it was the very first entry and I think the location was Pristina. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we find that where exactly? Not on the very first page at least. I have difficulties in finding. It's a meeting of the KiM Joint Command. Date 27th July. So it's not only August but it's also July. But that may not be the -- the meeting where Mr. Stanisic is reported to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 2nd of August is, as far as I can see now, but having a glance on the document, I do not see any location. Meeting is continued in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the 12th and 13th of August entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. 12th of August. That is on page 8 in e-court. Let me see. I do not see yet a location. As far as the 13th is concerned, I do not see any location either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think all the meetings -- I don't think it says a location in the notes but all the meetings of the command were held -- of the KiM Joint Command were held in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- at least that's the understanding of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And certainly Mr. Stanisic's understanding that he was in Greece and they certainly weren't held there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, one other point. Can Mr. Farr explain to us whether the document was received from the government of Serbia? In that case, do they have an RFA to which the government of Serbia responded, and if not, in what way was the document obtained. If there is any relevant evidence to that effect, we'd kindly ask to be informed of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, I think you told us already that you received it from the government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or at least you said it originated from the -- you didn't say, I think were those words that you obtained it. But at the same time what the gist of all this is, Mr. Farr seeks to undermine the value of the evidence of this witness in relation to what he says were Mr. Stanisic, his intents as far as the resolution of the Kosovo problem is concerned. The document is exclusively used for impeachment purposes. Now, the witness says, I wasn't involved. And the witness has not expressed himself on whether it's accurate or not what is written down here, but he says, more or less, in my assessment, I have not included this information, whether true or not true, but he has not considered that information. And he has then explained further what he meant when he said that Mr. Stanisic was rather peace-negotiation oriented than war oriented, what he understood to be war and not to be war, which is all relatively separate from what we find in the document. It's only the document triggered these observations. The witness did not in any way rely on them. So I'm just wondering what we are actually talking about at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I share Your Honour's query. From the Defence perspective we accept, or Mr. Stanisic accepts that the JSO was used in military action against the KLA, which we, the Defence, say was a terrorist organisation, and to that extent in our submission, the document is now of little value given that Mr. Farr has put those suggestions to the witness, the witness has responded. In our submission to put a huge document like this in front of the court with all these potential problems doesn't really add to the cross-examination exchange in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if Mr. Farr would have introduced his questions by, what would you say if reports would exist which says that Mr. Stanisic this and this and this which he is allowed to do, then we wouldn't need the whole document for the understanding of the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Unless Mr. Farr's case goes beyond Mr. Stanisic using the DB resources as a means of combatting the KLA, then since that is accepted between the parties, then -- and has been put to the witness, it seems that the document doesn't take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and apart from that it goes without conflict of course, it's just you are -- Mr. Farr, you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I was just going to say the concession is that it was used against the KLA but then part of it is also that the KLA was a terrorist organisation, which makes it sound like these were -- it's essentially allowing the Defence characterisation of this as being anti-terrorist operations, which has a connotation of police work. What the notes make clear is that this was in fact a military operation. This was an armed conflict. This was a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, any party inclined to include the whole of the Kosovo conflict into this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's what I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it was about impeachment, isn't it? You wanted to confront the witness with documentary evidence and where the documentary evidence in itself and the truth of it is not the basic thing to see. You are testing the assessment of this witness whether Mr. Stanisic was inclined to a more peaceful approach or that he would -- and I think -- it's a peaceful approach or that he would also take an option of the use of armed force in the Kosovo context. Let me try to explain it. I mean, the witness has answered those questions. I can even imagine that you wouldn't need the document anymore, so apart from whether it's authentic or not, because you said you would only use it for impeachment. Now, whatever you needed from the document to seek the impeachment of the witness, I think you've told him. Not -- of course, we'll fully research the authenticity and go into all the details, but that's not the point, is it? I'm looking at all three parties now. Both Prosecution and Defence. Prosecution in tendering it, Defence in so strongly objecting to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I thought you were with us then, Your Honour, but, yes, we agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Just one more point. This isn't an attempt to introduce the entire conflict. This is notes from six days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Farr, you are not going to explain that I think if you focus on ten days in August that I wanted to say that ten days in August is the whole of the conflict. Of course not. I mean, that doesn't need any further explanation. You have to understand my words, that is, are we going to -- are we going to discuss in the context of this case the armed conflict character of what happened in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Just more point, Your Honour. And perhaps I should have made this clear. The witness purports to understand the relationship between Stanisic and Milosevic, one aspect of that is the reason that he says Milosevic dismissed Stanisic. Stanisic's views on Kosovo are, therefore, relevant to this witness's understanding of the relationship between Milosevic and Stanisic. I didn't put that to him, but that's argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ruling of the Chamber: The document in itself used for impeachment reasons having heard the answers of the witness does not add probative value, and, therefore, it's not admitted. Not for any authenticity concerns, but just that for your exercise seeking to impeach the witness, that -- and you said that that is what you wanted to use the document for, that the probative value is not such that we should admit it. Therefore, admission is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the end of my examination. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a dramatic end, Mr. Farr. Mr. Petrovic, do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to put several questions to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Farr, this does not mean, and I also explained this to the Defence teams, that the non-admission doesn't mean that the answers the witness has given, triggered by quoting this document, that that evidence is in any way not there. It's there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's clear, Your Honour. Thank you. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in relation to the last line of questioning by my learned friend, can you tell us do you know if in 1998 the KLA at least according to the American State Department, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Was characterised as a terrorist organisation; right do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you also recall in the summer of 1998 -- the name of the State Department official is Robert Gelbard. I notice that it was missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and is the spelling as we find it on the transcript correct at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: G-e-l-b-a, I think. A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that at the time in the summer of 1998 almost 40 per cent of the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo was under the control of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous answer, at least I take it from the transcript has not been answered. Whether the witness is aware, Mr. Dragicevic, that the official from the State Department referred to the KLA as a terrorist organisation? Oh, now, I see there is a -- let me see, yes, it's a bit confusing, the question was answered, then you added to the name and then, of course, the question was answered. Apologies. Please proceed with your next question, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Witness, my learned friend began his examination today by asking you about the uniforms that you saw in the footage at Kula and during the hostage crisis. Do you distinguish between the various types of uniforms? Are you a person who would have any knowledge of the various patterns used for camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I was just an ordinary soldier and have no ability to draw that distinction. The only thing I can say is that at the review held in Kula, the unit that was lined up wore the so-called dress uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you distinguish between two types of camouflage uniforms? Are you able to draw that distinction?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, there is a clear suggestion in these questions that there may be different uniforms. If that's your point, then, of course, we would like to explore that. We have pictures of both and it might assist the Chamber that you point the differences. The witness has told us that from looking at it, it very much looked the same, and that seems not to be a thorough expert opinion on the matter, but if you see any difference between the two, please assist us and say look here the patches there or different colour or the -- that assists us more than further questions on this witness may not be the most appropriate person to make such distinction and that his layman's eye doesn't see at this moment from what he saw very briefly the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, but my learned friend's question was formulated in the same way. He saw one photograph at one time, then he saw another photograph and the question was were those uniforms identical. He couldn't make a comparison. He was simply asked whether they were identical so he expressed his views based on his layman skills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm asking your assistance. I'm asking your assistance. The Prosecution apparently wants to establish that the uniforms are the same. Now, with all relativity this witness not being an expert, the Prosecution asked, well, in your eyes was it the same, yes or no. Now, apparently you are challenging that. I mean, your question is saying you can't make a distinction, isn't it. There's a clear suggestion there that it's different and I'm seeking your assistance, show us, apart from what this witness can tell us about it, that the uniforms are clearly different. So that we can focus on that because without this challenge, you could, with all relativity, the evidence not given by an expert but with a layman's eye, you might be inclined to believe that the uniforms are the same, they look more or less the same, and if you are challenging that, we need your assistance to say look at that, look at that, look at that, so that we are better able to either follow the non-expert evidence and using our own layman's eye, or that you say no. If you look there, open our eyes for any difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand your suggestion but with your leave, I would like to proceed in the following way. I just wanted to get an answer from the witness whether he was ever involved in comparing uniforms, whether he had any skills in that respect. With your leave, the assistance that you are seeking we shall of course do our best to provide it to the Trial Chamber during our presentation of evidence. At this point in time, we don't think that this is an appropriate approach, we are happy with this answer but we do understand your need for us to research and explore this issue further on. I would then try, when we come to presenting our case, to provide appropriate photographs and comparisons if it is agreeable with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can the witness be shown document P3017.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It's a document, Mr. Dragicevic, that my learned friend showed to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we first look at page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this is a report compiled by an employee of the federal Ministry of the Interior on the 8th of August, 1992, as it says here. On this front page, do you see any incoming step, any protocol, register number, any indication at all confirming that this document was received by the competent service of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may look a little bit closely at the document. Thank you. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you see any designation indicating that the document was submitted and received?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These kind of documents are not submitted. Therefore, there is no official incoming stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: There is no incoming stamp at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Usually such a stamp is put on the right-hand side and it confirms that the document was received by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In the upper part of the document can you see any marks that would suggest that this document was sent by fax or by any similar means? Can you infer anything from that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You would agree that documents were sent by fax from one address to the other?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of that especially within I look at these red digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This is irrelevant because this was a designation made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we move to page 6 in Serbian and page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first few lines in the Serbian and for the benefit of the Chamber, it's the lower half of the page in English, where it reads that Ivanovic, aka Crnogorac, had a group numbering about 40 members who identified themselves as officials of the MUP of Serbia. My question for you is, do you know if the author of this report ever checked with the MUP of Serbia or the State Security of Serbia, whether Zivojin Ivanovic was really an official of the MUP of Serbia, or if he had any genuine connection with the ministry, or did he falsely represent and introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please try not to overlap. The interpreters didn't catch the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer because since there was no pause between question and answer, the interpreters were not able to translate your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer now? No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you aware that after the 1991 demonstrations in Belgrade that President Milosevic's security detail took over from the state security service, the public security service of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We used to have the so-called 2nd Administration which provided protections to the VIPs and facilities that was under the jurisdiction of the state security of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is the fact that Milosevic was engaging public security instead of state security illustrates the existence or the absence of Milosevic's trust vis-a-vis the state security department?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's clearly an invitation to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I rephrase my question, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that's a spontaneous offer, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: How do you understand the reasons that prompted Milosevic to have the public security station take over his security obligations and responsibilities post-1991 demonstration?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, same objection. In the absence of a foundation, it's still an invitation to speculate. There's no basis to believe that this witness would know why Milosevic made that decision or what the reasons were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then take it step by step. Are you familiar in any way with the reasons that prompted Milosevic to have the public security station take over his security and the responsibilities after the 1991 demonstration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understood it, that was only one of the elements that demonstrated President Milosevic's mistrust. I am sorry I just wanted to make a brief introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my first question is whether you are familiar with the reasons, then we'll further explore, or Mr. Petrovic will further explore what that familiarity is based on and then as a third step what those reasons were. First, are you familiar with the reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no proof for that and I don't know what the underlying reasons were. All I know is that it was done that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, there seems to be not a lot of basis for step two and step three. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know for how many years prior to 1992 the state security provided security services to presidents of the republic and other state dignitaries?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since I joined the State Security Services, the protection of VIPs and other dignitaries was within the jurisdiction of a special administration within the service that was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Minutes ago you mentioned a 2nd Administration. Now, are we really talking about the 6th Administration within the state security department that was in charge of providing the protection of VIP, that it has this specialised duty?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a second section and I had some other section in mind, but, yes, you are right, we are actually talking about the 6th Administration of the state security of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Mr. Witness, are you aware that after the dismissal of Mr. Stanisic in 1998, were the ranks introduced in the State Security, Service introduced for the first time after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know that after the departure of Mr. Stanisic, the key points in the service were filled by members from the public security service?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in the speech that you analysed yesterday with my learned friend, the speech read out by Mr. Simatovic in Kula, there was mention of 1991 and the 2nd Administration. Would you agree with me that in 1991, the 2nd Administration did not exist at all in the state security department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters have not heard the answer. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you mentioned your encounter with Captain Dragan in 2000, if I'm not mistaken, during the October coup. Do you know if Captain Dragan took place in these turmoil events that took place in October 2000, and if you know, on whose side was he?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I heard that he sided with the forces that were against Milosevic who carried out the coup.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's time to take a break. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 25 minutes. Then we'll take a break, but before doing so, Mr. Jordash, the Chamber would be assisted by knowing the last known address of the witness we talked about earlier, so as to finalise -- to give follow-up on your oral application.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A member of my team tried to call him this morning and spoke to somebody in his office and we are waiting for him to call back, so there's instructions to obtain his address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00 and expect you to finish by quarter past 11.00, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, apologies for the delayed start. Mr. Jordash, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, I want to just return to a matter that my learned friend for the Prosecution dealt with yesterday at the close of the day and it's the issue relating to the relationship between Milosevic and Stanisic. And my learned friend dealt with it generally, or in a general sense at page 14885 of the transcript, and put to you that at line 21: [As read] "We can agree on that basis, i.e., on the basis that Stanisic had kept his position from 1992 until 1998 that whatever their subjective feelings for each, Milosevic and Stanisic worked together professionally and effectively." And my learned friend asked you in a general sense: "In other words Milosevic valued and appreciated Stanisic's work." And you said: "Well, if you view it that way, yes." I want to have you clarify that answer as compared to some of the comments you made in your statement concerning the mistrust between the two. And I don't want to deal with it in a general way, I want you to try to give some concrete examples concerning your view that there was mistrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we please turn to the witness's statement at D466.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At paragraph 85 where you say: [As read] "I think that Stanisic managed to keep his position because Milosevic was smart enough to keep someone on that position who was good in his job. Stanisic was from the DB and had a good team." Now, of course it's a legitimate question as to how and why Stanisic kept his job, especially in light of what you say was mistrust between the two. Could you try to clarify how that mistrust manifested itself from what you observed in the years between 1992 and 1998? What conversations were you having or what were you observing? Could you make this as concrete as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Milosevic was intelligent enough as a human being and politician to make sure that he did not get rid of individuals who were professionals and dedicated to their work that easily, especially if they were people who would try to perform any task they were given in the best possible way. Let me give you a few examples to illustrate what I've just said and to support my belief of there having been mistrust on Milosevic's part vis-a-vis Stanisic. It was already stated here that the 6th Administration, charged with the protection of VIPs, provided its services to all leaders and very important persons, VIPs, whenever it was called upon to do so. Milosevic changed all that. Instead of hiring people from state security, he drew upon people from the Ministry of the Interior and even his personal escort was a policeman. Should I give his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senta Milenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just pause you there. In relation to other VIPs what was the situation, was it only Milosevic who received security from outside of the state security?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, only Milosevic. No one else. The 6th Administration serviced everybody else. The second example, on the night when Mr. Stanisic flew to Bosnia in order to obtain from Mr. Radovan Karadzic a document to the effect that he was withdrawing from politics and all the positions he held, the weather was terrible and his life was at risk. I stayed behind at Uzicka Street villa and I remember that Mr. Holbrooke had already gone back to the American embassy. Those left behind with me were Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milan Milutinovic. At one point Mr. Milosevic took my arm in his and suggested that we should take a walk in the garden. As we were strolling, he asked me what it was that we also discussed with the Americans, with the CIA at Langley. My answer was that I had drawn up a report on this matter and that the president was given a copy of it. I said that I had one objection to make and Milosevic asked me what it was that you can object with the president of a state. I said that I drew up the report in one copy only and that I'd like to have that copy back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm limited in time. I want to really stay on the focus. What do you mean when you say that Milosevic or what do you mean when you imply that Milosevic appreciated Stanisic's work? Which work are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Milosevic highly appreciated the professional work exhibited by Mr. Stanisic as an intelligence officer, as well as a counter-intelligence, topnotch analyst who had the political flair as well. After all, he had a degree in political science and was an educated man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You describe in your statement a cat-and-mouse relationship between Milosevic and Stanisic. That's at paragraph 70. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point I wouldn't be able to tell you who had the role of mouse and who of the cat. However, there was this constant game of upmanship where Stanisic insisted on concrete issues that he believed he was right about and that needed to be appreciated, and on the other hand the manipulations that politicians are normally given to engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At paragraph 72 you discuss the Kula award ceremony and you note that in the last three sentences: "There were a lot of people around Milosevic who were against the DB and he alone was rather distrustful, and perhaps in a way that celebration was supposed to improve the position of the service." In which way was that celebration supposed to improve the position?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were certainly a great deal of suspicion around at the time. I can state upon full responsibility that the State Security Service was one of the most respectable institutions in the country, one which was fully aware of the job it was doing and what sort of job it was. That's something I would not be able to say of other institutions. There was a great deal of resistance to state security on the part of some individuals, it was just the human nature, I don't know. At any rate, there was a great deal of suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which individuals had this distrust, or, sorry, a good deal of resistance?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean above all the circle of people around President Milosevic, politicians. I'm not sure about the army. At any rate, primarily people from the political circle around President Milosevic and from the Socialist Party of Serbia. And if I may be allowed to explain, my understanding of the ceremony at Kula, I believe that the ceremony was conceived in such a way that Milosevic should be impressed by it, by our intention to create a modern centre and put together an anti-terrorist unit that would be equal to all similar units world-wide, a unit that would be bent on fighting international terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it significant or not that, as you've said in your statement at paragraph 84, that the service, according to Stanisic, was not supposed to interfere with politics? Was it significant that Stanisic wasn't a politician?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was one of the main points that I personally agreed with, if I can be allowed to give my opinion. To this day, I believe that every service must be outside of politics, though in part I can say that none of the services --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- was it significant that Stanisic wasn't a member of the SPS? Please answer concretely, I'm running out of time.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In which way? From what you observed, what you saw, what you heard.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you don't belong to a single political party then you'll allow me to say then you enjoy a bit more freedom than everybody else in doing your job concretely. If you are tied to a party, then you are bound by the decisions of the party leadership. I had been a member of the Yugoslav League of Communists, when the party ceased to exist, I did not join another and have not in fact to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Just to finish off Kula award issue, did you receive an award?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. A wrist-watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What for? Why?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. If you view the footage from Kula, I can't -- I don't know if you heard -- if you were able to hear what was being said there but when my name was read out, Mr. Stanisic asked and what was it that you got this award for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you a member of the anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't. Perhaps it was for my contribution to the organisation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Kosovo. We heard that -- or you testified that the US State Department had designated the KLA as a terrorist organisation. Now, putting aside the United States designation, are you able to testify as to why the state security or Stanisic considered the KLA at that point in time to be a terrorist organisation? What you saw and what you heard is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have firsthand experience because I did not go to Kosovo to be able to witness specific activities and KLA actions, but on TV you were able to see fully-armed units with full gear who were engaged in terrorist activities, attacks on the civilian population, and attempts to cleanse huge areas of Kosovo of any Serbs whilst at the same time committing atrocities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I have, please, on the screen 1D05246.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this is a visit of the CIA to, I think, Belgrade. Perhaps you can assist with this.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the visit to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In May of 1996?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you part of this visit and meeting of intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 1 -- to page 4 of the B/C/S and page 1D082206 of the English. Perhaps this shouldn't -- this should be under seal. There are some names in it which ought not to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I only want to go to this page because it just contextualises the report and deals with the visit of the, as you can see there on the screen, the visit of a respective person from the CIA. And then if we move over to the B/C/S page 7 and 1D082209 of the English, and it's a report there of what Stanisic is reporting to the CIA in 1996. And you can see there Jovica Stanisic said that: [As read] "He just returned from Pristina so he was in a position to provide information on the merit. Having given a short description of the terrorist actions in Decani, Stemunje [phoen], Peja and the village of Sipolje near Kosovska Mitrovica, he said that these are synchronised acts of Albanian extremists, which is collaborated [sic] by the fact that they occurred within the time interval of only about 40 minutes. He said that it would be a dangerous task to destabilise the local area, Serbia, and the entire country." Then Stanisic goes on to, during this meeting, disclose the names of various officials who in his view the instigators of these crimes and then later on refers to the so-called president of Kosovo's government in exile Bujar Bukoshi. Were you present when Stanisic was reporting terrorist actions to the CIA?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In contact with a representative of the CIA in Belgrade, we furnished information and evidence in support of our statements that such activities were indeed happening in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go over to the next page, please. That's page, I think, 8 of the B/C/S and 1D082210. And again we won't refer to the name, but you can see halfway down the page in the English there's a name mentioned, senior member of the CIA, "... reiterated that they are concerned about the possibility of an escalation of terrorism in Kosovo, the outbreak of conflict that would lead to armed conflicts and the intervention of the Yugoslav Army ... And especially the expansion of the crisis to neighbouring countries. In this context, he singled out Macedonia and predicated that the arrival of hundreds of thousands of Albanian refugees could destabilise the situation in that country. Jovica Stanisic agreed with these findings and pointed out that a potential armed rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija, Albanians would have no chance and besides they are not ready for war." Were you there during that discussion when that particular American CIA agent agreed with the assessment of an escalation of terrorism in Kosovo? You still with us?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you there during this discussion?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I paused because you were talking. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And can you recall what was said about the concerns of the intervention of the Yugoslav Army into the conflict or into the situation?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the American side was particularly concerned or worried by the Army of Yugoslavia. Were there to be a crisis or military conflicts as Mr. Stanisic said, the ethnic Albanians would not stand a chance but that would, at the same time, expose the civilian population to a great deal of suffering. The conflict would probably spill over to the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and there were conflicts brewing in that part of Greece which is known as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which part of Greece, what was the name of the --

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chameria [In English] The northern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To wrap up this subject, let's go back to your statement in paragraph 87 and 88 you discuss there Stanisic and his conflict with Milosevic over the issue. Can you just in two sentences or three sentences just summarise the core of that conflict over Kosovo, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the initial events, Milosevic opted for the use of force and this was the main reason why he came into conflict with Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Stanisic had contacts with certain leaders of the Kosovo Albanians and I still fully agree with his views. I think he was right. It was possible through -- to solve the crisis through negotiations and discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How often was Stanisic leading with Kosovan Albanian leaders at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Stanisic meet with any American officials in Belgrade concerning the issue about how to resolve the Kosovan crisis or how to prevent it escalating?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost every meeting Mr. Stanisic had with representatives of the American administration had to do with the crisis in Kosovo, and with how to resolve the crisis in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Over which period of time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it applied to the early days from the first indications of the conflict in Kosovo through to the end of Stanisic's term of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we just go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm almost finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just to clarify one final issue which I don't think we've really specified in the type of detail that I hope we can. The issue of force. You just said that Milosevic wanted to use force, on the other hand we've seen documents which show that the JSO was involved in the use of force. Could you try to clarify what the distinction was between the approach Stanisic wanted to take in relation to force and the approach that Milosevic wanted to take in relation to force?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on Milosevic's approach to this notion because I'm not fully aware of what he was thinking. I can only speak about Mr. Stanisic's approach. It was based on the principle of pure anti-terrorist combat, which is the principle applied by each and every country in the world. That means, in other words, to annihilate the terrorists and to proceed thereafter with political negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, were there any political murders that you are aware of during Stanisic's reign as chief of the state security, and the second question was: Was there any after he resigned?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure, because I was in the service at the time, that while Mr. Stanisic was chief of the State Security Service there were no murders of that kind. After his departure and after General Markovic was installed in that position, assassinations started taking place in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what Stanisic's relationship was like with Djindjic before his unfortunate murder?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this doesn't arise from cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, in our submission, it does. The Prosecution have tried to link through this case in general Stanisic with political or the activities of the JSO after his resignation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think the issue is Mr. Farr says it doesn't arise from cross-examination, not that it may not be relevant in the case as such. Could you indicate where this matter was touched upon in cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, there was a discussion between my learned friend and the witness concerning Djindjic and the timing of this witness's resignation and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is my last question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is my last question, could you just answer that question: Do you know what the relationship was like between Stanisic and Djindjic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they had an extremely good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you believe that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions I saw Mr. Djindjic in the office of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I would have just one matter briefly, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Farr:

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sir, during cross-examination by Mr. Petrovic you were asked whether you were aware that after the dismissal of Mr. Stanisic in 1998 ranks were introduced in the State Security Service for the first time after the Second World War. And you said, "Yes, I am aware of that." When we watched the Kula video yesterday we saw Zika Ivanovic and Radojica Bozovic both being introduced as colonels, and then following that in a portion of the video that we didn't watch, a number of other men are introduced as colonels, there are then lieutenant-colonels, captains, and so on down the ranks. Can you explain, I guess, your answer that there were no ranks in light of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that the special operations unit was a military unit and it had ranks. Members of the State Security Service, however, were people in civilian clothes and we didn't have any ranks. I personally was against that. We just had titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So ranks existed in the JSO but not in the rest of the DB; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would renew my motion for the admission of P -- sorry, of 65 ter 4777.1. That's the document that the Chamber ruled on immediately before the break, and I'm renewing my motion because I believe circumstances have changed. The issue of Kosovo was explored quite extensively and I would just call the Chamber's attention to one answer in particular, page 42, beginning at line 2, the witness was asked about Mr. Stanisic's approach in relation to force, he said: "It was based on the principle of pure anti-terrorist combat which is the principle applied by each and every country in the world. That means, in other words, to annihilate the terrorists and to proceed thereafter what political negotiations with a view to finding peaceful solutions." In my submission, that makes the admission of 4777.1, as impeachment, appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just briefly take instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would remove our objection if I can ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's an offer there, but Mr. Petrovic, would you take -- would you also have one question and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I still stand by to everything I said and I really cannot discern any change in the situation based on Mr. Jordash's questions. His questions can be formulated in the same way like Mr. Farr's questions, so this document is not helpful at all. It will remain in evidence and it will be the subject of your evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And Your Honour, just to be clear, I'm offering it for the same person, for impeachment only. I'm not offering it as a basis for conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear any objection to Mr. Jordash asking an additional question. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Further re-examination by Mr. Jordash:

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Staying with the subject of Kosovo, do you know anything about Al-Qaeda in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is withdrawn, I do understand, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objections still standing as expressed by Mr. Petrovic and will admit into evidence the document and has taken notice of the Prosecution telling us that it is still seeking admission for impeachment purposes at this moment. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There was one issue from yesterday which was the 47th extended session of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could please perhaps first deal with this one or is there any ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, no, I apologise. I jumped the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we have to do all the formalities for admitting it into evidence. Madam Registrar, the number of the document which is, let me have a look --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4777.1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3046, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to have it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of, but I would prefer to check that just to be sure, so perhaps provisionally under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3046 is admitted provisionally under seal, Mr. Farr, could we hear from you say within the next 24 or 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We do not object to the Prosecution tendering the 65 ter 6303 which is the 47th extended session of the FRY Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection either, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record we have uploaded the portions only the portions that we rely on that we indicated to the Defence counsel yesterday as 6303.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be any need for further contextualization to have other portions we'll hear from you, but may I take it that you accept this limitation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, 65 ter 6303.1 would receive number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P3047, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And any need to have it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'd prefer to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3047 is admitted provisionally under seal. Same time-limit applies, Mr. Farr. Is there any other matter in relation to documents used or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There is, will but there's a long list I don't think there's any need to detain the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we don't need to keep the witness for that purpose. Mr. Dragicevic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As matters stand now we have no witness for next week, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I am, I guess, hoping that the witness who is scheduled next may avoid the -- may come of his own volition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say then this might resolve the problem of having no witness. There is no alternative scenario so that we could use our time in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The alternative scenario is the UN personnel who -- I forget his, DST-069, who again is subject to -- not again, who is presently subject to a subpoena, we are trying to contact his ministry again in the hope that he will not require a service of it, but will actually, again, get on a plane and be here for next week. But apart from that, I think we have run out of witnesses. I think we have some -- one or two, I think, outstanding 92 bis applications and then we have our proposed expert for the Mladic diaries, and also a prominent witness from England who we've indicated to the court that we wish to apply to have them attend out of turn and probably during or after the Simatovic case, so that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we have some uncertainties here now, and of course this raises another question that is where the Simatovic stands in preparing its case presentation. I mean, we have at least one where you applied to be able to call the witness after the Simatovic Defence had started. And of course, we urged the Simatovic Defence to prepare for the start of their case presentation. Under the present circumstance, of course, we cannot be sure that we are not losing a lot of time up until the moment when you have presented your last witness, so, therefore, the Chamber is even more -- more than it was before interested in where the Simatovic Defence stands as far as the preparation of their case presentation is concerned. Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just indicate in relation to the two outstanding witnesses, DST-060 and DST-069, those that we -- if they were here we could call, it may well be that we can finish those in three days. I'm speculating, but certainly in relation to DST-060, we do not intend to spend more than 45 minutes in addition to his 92 ter statement, if he arrives here. And in relation to DST-069, he has a voluminous transcript and I suspect that he is not going to be the most contentious of witnesses to say the least.
