So it may well be that if we lose next week, we could still, in substance, finish the Stanisic Defence the week after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witnesses are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, of course, what I'm inquiring about, where the Simatovic stands in preparing for their case presentation. I mean, if they would not appear, if we would have another empty week and another empty week, of course we would have to seriously consider to see whether the remaining witnesses, once they appear, that they could be heard even if that would be after the start of the Simatovic Defence case presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would have no objection to whatever keeps the trial moving, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I'm not anticipating on any decisions yet, but I'm just inquiring in how we can proceed without losing time. And that's the reason why I address the Simatovic Defence at this moment where we earlier urged them to seriously prepare for their case presentation, where we stand and what could be done if the situation would arise that we can't hear any Stanisic evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our Defence team are doing our best to get ready for starting our case. You are aware of our problems that date back to the earlier period. However, we believe that we can accommodate the Trial Chamber with their intention to avoid wasting time, or rather, wasting weeks while we wait for specific witnesses. I think that within the next two weeks it will be unrealistic to expect us to call our first witness. It would also be useful and beneficial to us if we were not on stand-by next week in anticipation of a possible appearance of a witness which would give us some spare time to prepare ourselves better for our Defence case and the examination of our first witness. Therefore, at this point I think it is not realistic to expect us to begin our examination of witnesses before the week starting on the 28th, specifically because certain unpredicted things happened in the meantime, we expect a 92 bis witness to appear plus another two witnesses, and we counted upon on that to happen within the next two weeks. And I also think that in that category is the undefined status of a protected witness, an OTP witness, for whom the Stanisic Defence team requested to be recalled and examined in relation to the Mladic diary. So before the 28th we are technically not in a position to start calling our witnesses. However, it would be beneficial to us to know if there were no witnesses in the next two weeks, I, myself, and my colleagues have some free time to become and get prepared better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes. On the 3rd of November we sent an e-mail to the attention of the Simatovic Defence requesting information about the order for the first five witnesses. To the best of my knowledge we didn't receive a response. I think that that would be very helpful to our preparation if we could receive that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are saying you are just asking for the order, not the date on which --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would add one question to that. You are talking about 92 bis witnesses. Have statements been taken and are they on paper at this moment, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe I wasn't precise enough. I was not referring to our 92 bis witnesses, but rather the witnesses called by the Stanisic Defence and it was decided today not to recall them for cross-examination. All these circumstances have improved our situation in terms of our accelerating our work. Now, as regards to the remark raised by Ms. Marcus, it is no problem, we see no problem for us to send in the shortest possible time the list of witnesses starting from the 28th onwards until the recess begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say you see no problem to send in the shortest possible time. What is the shortest possible time? Is that this week, is that Monday, Tuesday? I'd like to have concrete information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we were not working next week and if my colleague and I can go on the required trips in the field, I think that at the beginning of the week after we can give you the list of witnesses that we intend to start with. And besides we have no objection to the Mladic's diary expert be examined either during or after our case, but if you allow me, I would like to express our opinion with regard to the Prosecution witness. Now, for clarity, I would kindly ask for us to go to a private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will do that, but first, what Ms. Marcus is asking is the order of the first five witnesses. So we start with A, then B, C, D, E. Would that really need another ten days? I mean, they can start inquiring in the background of those witnesses, they can see whether they have testified before, what is known about them, so as to start the preparation. I take it that's what you want?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: She is not asking for the full list at this moment, but at least to know in which order the first five will appear. Is there any way you can provide that earlier than in ten days from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, tomorrow is Friday and if we are not working next week I'm going to check on Monday already with the witnesses that we intend to call according to certain sequence, whether they are able to come over and after that we can provide Ms. Marcus with a list. But before that we have to check all the logistical issues involved and whether all these witnesses are really ready to travel and come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- I can imagine that even if it's not certain yet whether finally that order would be followed, Ms. Marcus would be happy to receive in which order you are going to ask these witnesses to come and then it may well be that one is not available or another one is not available, but at least that you have some guidance as to where to start. Ms. Marcus, is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we need to know, perhaps in the way that the Stanisic Defence did. They put in order, at times that order had to be changed, we tried to be flexible. But we would like to see the order that you anticipate as soon as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When could you provide what you have at this moment on your mind as the order you would wish -- the order in which you would wish the witnesses to appear? Could you already provide Ms. Marcus with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, if it is acceptable for Ms. Marcus we can have it ready for her on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, would that assist?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked for us to go briefly to a private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any other matters? Any other matter to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only seeking some guidance. We received, I think, an e-mail in informal communication from the Chamber concerning the expectation that we would not, I think, seek to admit -- apologies if I don't get this completely accurate, but I think the gist of it was that we shouldn't seek to admit evidence during the Simatovic case or subsequently that we ought to have admitted during our case. The position is this: That we considered long and hard about filing another application for an adjournment because we have received a huge amount of disclosure over the last six weeks, I think in excess of 100.000 pages. There is, before the Prosecution jump up, no criticism of the Prosecution, it's just 66(B) requests and material from other cases and so on. Having considered whether to an apply for an adjournment, we took the view that the better approach, especially bearing in mind Mr. Stanisic's health, was to review that material during our own case and continue reviewing it during the Simatovic case and then seek to have admitted any evidence we discover in that -- discover from that disclosure on perhaps an on-going basis, which doesn't mean to say that we'll be bombarding the Chamber with applications. We'll obviously do it in a sensible way, but we would hope that Your Honour would appreciate that way of proceeding rather than having to deal with another application to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are putting a marker here to say where the Chamber expects you not to start presenting evidence once you have finished, apart from that one exception of course, I hint that the possibility that there may be other instances, although we'd really like to not to seek you to go on presenting your case, that you say in view of disclosure over the last six weeks, not blaming the Prosecution, which of course also raises a question whether all these requests for this material to be disclosed was timely done, but let's not discuss it at this moment but I just put that. You put a marker here and say that if that material triggers any need to call any further evidence, we might ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record. I'm not in any way anticipating on how we would react to that, but it's clear that you would rather not have your hands bound by that guidance of the Chamber in view of this specific material, and whether your hands are still bound or not will be decided once we have received any application in this respect. And you already indicate that such applications would mainly rely on recently disclosed material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, we intend to file bar table motions in the next - we hope - in the next two weeks in relation to our 65 ter list. It's material which hasn't as yet made it on there that we are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see how matters develop. I'm not granting anything in any way at this moment, any application will be seriously considered by the Chamber, and we have given our main ideas on this matter in the earlier communication with the Defence. That is, no new evidence after, that's our main, and you say we might nevertheless apply for specific material to take a different approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. Nothing else? Then -- yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The witness stated that he was from -- sorry, the witness stated that from 1975 to 1979 he worked for the state security of the Republic of Serbia. In 1985, the witness started working for the federal State Security Service. In late 1992, the witness became special advisor to the chief of the service before progressing to the head of the 9th Administration. In 1997 he became the assistant chief of the DB. The witness testified that he met with representatives of foreign services and reported back to Mr. Stanisic. If necessary, Stanisic would also meet with the representatives. During the time that Stanisic was chief, the service raised its contacts with foreign services from around 40 to around 60 states. The situation deteriorated once Stanisic was fired in 1998. The witness described meeting a number of people from the CIA. The first contact between Stanisic and the CIA was secret and took place in early 1992. The witness was also present. They discussed how to resolve certain situations and how to assist the CIA in collecting information. The policy of the service was to emphasise contact and co-operation with other countries. Following the signing of the peace agreement in Dayton, the witness together with Stanisic went to Zagreb to discuss the implementation of the Dayton Accords. The witness describes the hostage crisis that occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995 where United Nations personnel were captured and used as human shields to forestall NATO attacks. The accused Stanisic was responsible for the negotiations with the Republika Srpska state leadership. The negotiations succeeded and in early June of 1995, the first convoy was taken out of Bosnia and into Serbia. Over 450 soldiers were eventually freed and transferred into safety. The witness also described the accused Stanisic and the State Security Service's participation in the liberation of the French pilots captured in Republika Srpska in the second half of 1995. Stanisic also participated in the liberation of a journalist, David Rohde from Christian Science Monitor. The witness also testified to participating in secret operations together with the CIA and representatives of the FRY Ministry of Foreign Affairs in locating or searching for potential mass graves in Eastern Bosnia. The witness also stated that in 1996, the State Security of Serbia detained Erdemovic for war crimes and arranged his delivery to The Hague Tribunal. The witness escorted Erdemovic to The Hague. The witness believed that Milosevic's attitude toward the State Security Service and Stanisic was characterised by mistrust. The witness testified to the relationship between Stanisic and Milosevic. The State Security of Serbia was not responsible for Milosevic's service -- sorry, security. Finally, the witness was in charge of the protocol in the Kula ceremony of 1997. He believed that the point of the ceremony was to show Milosevic that they had a modern unit to fight against terrorism and to improve the position of the state security in Milosevic's eyes. According to the witness, the accused Stanisic was a professional who did not belong to any political party. He directed the work of the service towards combating nationalism and did not express discriminatory behaviour within his role. Stanisic insisted that rules, especially procedure regarding obtaining approvals for measures such as phone tapping, be obeyed. The witness believed the direct cause of Stanisic's dismissal was a clash with Milosevic regarding the approach to the Kosovan crisis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. And then we'll inform the parties and the public after having heard from Mr. Jordash when we actually will resume.
